title: SCOTUS has done some “crazy things,” Sotomayor says
author: Nora Collins
content:
The new year will bring a new side job for Justice Clarence Thomas. The Daily Texan reported that he “will teach a course at UT’s School of Civic Leadership to 17 UT undergraduate students in spring 2027,” drawing on “texts by civil rights activists and political figures.” Although Supreme Court justices often teach seminars at law schools, it’s rare for them to take part in a course aimed at undergrads, according to The Daily Texan.

At the Court

On Friday, the justices met in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. That afternoon, the Supreme Court announced that, during the conference, the justices added a new case to the oral argument docket: Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, on whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes. For more on the case, see the On Site section below.

Additional orders from Friday’s conference are expected this morning at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the court to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request has been fully briefed since Oct. 30, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

title: The resignation of Jensen Huang from Nvidia and everything that has followed
author: @pcgamer
content:
Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, has resigned as President, CEO, and member of the board, effective immediately. That is the message which was posted this morning on the Nvidia newsroom.

Get to the latest updates

He has been at the centre of a big ol' scandal since last week, which threatened his position at the head of one of the biggest companies in the world. It started with a report over his relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, which moved into him emailing his entire workforce to say sorry that he's had an affair (though didn't name the person), an invite to talk to national security and foreign affairs officials in US Congress next week, and now reports of potentially a second affair, this time with an Nvidia employee, have come to light.

This is what sparked the emergency board meeting last night which has culminated in his resignation from all sectors of the company.

Nvidia CFO, Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO, while the company searches for a permanent replacement for Jensen, with Harvey C. Jones appointed the first ever chair of Nvidia's board of directors.

"Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Nvidia, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer," reads the statement on the Nvidia newsroom. "Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates."

“Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, Nvidia. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

There has so far been no statement from Jensen himself on the matter, but the Nvidia statement thanks him for his service...

"Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

Latest updates

2026-11-12T23:05:26.795Z

It is understood that Jensen has agreed to testify at the US Congress in response to the letter from last week which invited him to attend "a joint, closed-door briefing on Nvidia’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang."

Multiple reports, from CBS and Politico among others, are noting that he will attend and the date of the meeting is now being arranged. The original date in the letter was November 18, and it is understood that it will at least be taking place ahead of the Thanksgiving break.

According to the BBC, "Florida Representative Brian Mast says that Huang indicated he is willing to appear, adding that his resignation as Nvidia CEO "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony."

2026-11-12T22:55:40.939Z

There's seemingly a lot of sadness, sympathy, or praise around the resignation of Jensen Huang—and I have to say I've not seen a whole lot of sympathy for Lori Huang—but so far we have not seen any actual reaction from fellow execs in terms of any kind of protest. Whether we'll see any Nvidia staffers following him out of the Santa Clara campus, or its other campuses around the world, we may have to wait and see.

2026-11-12T22:33:27.334Z

Brian Catanzaro, vice president of appliced deep learning research at Nvidia, and one of the leading brains (brians?) behind Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS) has noted his sadness that Jensen Huang is no longer leading Nvidia after his resignation today.

2026-11-12T20:54:45.983Z

Jensen reportedly had an affair with a second Nvidia employee

Reuters reports that Jensen was engaged in an affair with a second Nvidia employee, according to "two people familiar with the matter," putting the ousted CEO on a two-day streak of extramarital revelations. Reuters has elected not to name the second Nvidia employee, who the outlet was unsuccessful in attempting to contact. We'll have to see if a third emerges—but at this point, it's not like Jensen can be any more resigned.

2026-11-12T17:54:07.041Z

Intel is a cautionary tale for Nvidia's board

It's not going to be easy to find a replacement for Jensen Huang, and Intel is a prime example of how jumping between CEOs can lead to stagnation.

Here's Andy on Intel's revolving door of CEOs and how hard it will be to find someone right for Nvidia's top job.

"Whoever leads Nvidia next will step into truly gigantic shoes, and in the face of an AI market that looks increasingly wobbly, they'll need to be the right person for the job. And swapping leaders out on the regular? Well, it's taken its toll on Intel over the years, that's for sure."

2026-11-12T16:54:59.694Z

Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia interim CEO?

In his quick profile of new interim CEO, Colette Kress, Jacob notes that "you might be excused as a gamer for never hearing about her; an earnings call isn't everybody's cup of tea.

"Colette Kress has been chief financial officer at Nvidia since 2013. That's 13 years sat alongside Jensen in calls with investors and financial institutions to discuss how the company is doing. Kress has been in the role for the record highs of recent years, and the not-so-record lows of others, like the price plummets of '25, '21, and '18.

"Prior to her role at Nvidia, Kress was SVP and CFO at Cisco for a couple of years and Corporate VP at Microsoft for nearly five. She also worked at Texas Instruments—all the big hitters, then."

2026-11-12T16:24:05.150Z

Just to note, Jensen's departure from Nvidia doesn't mean good things for PC gaming

Our Andy has written a considered take on what Nvidia and Jensen parting ways, and especially a new CEO coming in, will mean for PC gamers. And the short of it is: nothing good. Jensen built the company with his co-founders to create computer graphics accelerators that made all your games look awesome™️and while he and the company have moved towards another road he knew that's what Nvidia was built on.

Anyone else coming into the company isn't going to have that level of attachment to PC gaming. And certainly looking at the bottom of the balance sheet is not going to be paying much attention to it, either. It's AI all the way, and we've got to hope the GeForce team inside Nvidia keeps pushing for attention and resources in this new era.

2026-11-12T16:12:16.852Z

Chairman of the Select Committee on China, John Moolenaar, is not mincing his words in this latest statement on the resignation of Jensen Huang. He says: "Nvidia must now change its corporate practices and appoint leadership that makes national security its top priority."

2026-11-12T15:56:57.553Z

If you're after a full breakdown of the timeline surrounding Jensen's departure, our Jacob Ridley has put together an excellent blow-by-blow account of how it all went down.

2026-11-12T15:36:01.331Z

Trump wants Tim Cook

Donald Trump has spoken up about his buddy Jensen's resignation, stating that there is only one person for the job: former Apple CEO, Tim Cook. Trump has always spoken very positively about Cook in the past, most especially when talking about his first term in office where he was very impressed with himself "to have the head of Apple calling to 'kiss my ass'" after a phonecall from Cook.

2026-11-12T15:31:40.705Z

CNN correspondent for AI, Hadas Gold, has posted on X what she says are the emails sent out to Nvidia employees today from new CEO, Colette Kress, and its first chair of the board, Harvey Jones. There will apparently be a company meeting on November 18, the same day as Jensen is supposed to visit the US Congress.

2026-11-12T15:26:52.291Z

Who can replace Jensen?

As interim CEO we have, as many predicted (including our Jacob Fox) the current Nvidia chief financial officer, Colette Kress. As a short term measure it makes sense for the board to go straight for the money person who's been talking with investors at earnings calls for 13 years now. That's the way to help calm a volatile market, and one that is likely to be spooked losing one of the main proponents for AI.

But what about the long term appointment? Nvidia's board has reportedly employed an outside agency to aid in identifying candidates for the CEO position, but who would want that job? We've got some thoughts as to who might make a good fit, but whether any of them would be keen, or whether the board would be keen on them, is another matter.

  • Lip-Bu Tan - CEO, Intel
  • Lisa Su - CEO, AMD
  • Rene Haas - CEO, Arm
  • Elon Musk - CEO, Tesla, SpaceX
  • Tim Cook - Executive chairman and ex-CEO, Apple

2026-11-12T15:02:36.910Z

Reaction to his resignation

Tim Sweeney inevitably has something to say on the matter, as does Clement Delangue, co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face.

Jim Cramer, host of Mad Money on CNBC had this to say:

2026-11-12T14:30:53.190Z

Nvidia's share price has now dropped 13% in pre-market trading.

2026-11-12T14:26:13.183Z

Tim Sweeney said it "would be an Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy" to fire Jensen Huang from his position as CEO. He suggests it would do grievous harm to the US.

Not holding back, he also said it would be a "ridiculous shitshow... to replace one of the leading technology visionaries of the modern era with the company's money guy."

Elon Musk just said it would be "an honor" to hire Jensen. I'm sure it would, Elon. I'm sure it would.

2026-11-12T14:20:51.713Z

Here is a brief timeline of events which kicked off last week with a story by the New York times into Jensen's relationship with Alice Huang.

  • October 29 - New York Times report comes out covering the relationship with an alleged foreign intelligence asset.
  • November 5 - Jensen is called to a meeting with various foreign affairs and national security committee leaders in US Congress, set for November 18.
  • November 8 - Jensen sends an email to all Nvidia staff, also published on the company newsroom, admitting to and apologising for an affair. The board also posts a statement on the newsroom saying it was launching an internal investigation.
    • Nvidia share price drops - around 21% since October 28
  • November 9 - Donald Trump speaks to press about Jensen, backing the CEO. "He's an amazing guy. I just hope there's no problem. If there is a problem, we'll let you know about it."
  • November 10 - Law firms chase investors to sign up for class action lawsuits or 'investigations' into the company. We've seen at least five press releases of lawyers offering their services to investors. Nvidia itself hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead the internal investigation.
    • The Information reports Alice Huang facilitated some 240,000 AI GPUs, costing around $7.5B, to be accessed by Chinese companies.
    • Axios reports that Howard Lutnick was sent a classified warning memo over the relationship between Jensen and Alice Huang. Noting that Marco Rubio also warned Trump just before they picked up Jensen en route to the China trip
  • November 11 - Reports surface that Jensen had a second affair, with an internal Nvidia employee, Kimberly Powell. An emergency board meeting is convened to determine Jen-Hsun's fate as CEO.
    • Nvidia's share price plumets even further, to lowest value since June 2025.
  • November 12 - Jensen Huang resigns from all positions at Nvidia with CFO Colette Kress taking over the role of interim CEO while the company looks for a successor.

title: After 28 years, Nintendo unintentionally recast the actor behind Navi in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake to preserve "the feel of the original"
author: Kaan Serin
content:
Listen!

For The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's shiny new remake, Nintendo unintentionally cast the same actor twice - 28 years apart - to deliver Navi's infamous "Heys!" and "Listens!"

The Switch 2's Ocarina of Time makes a pretty substantial change to the N64's Ocarina of Time, released almost three decades prior. There's proper voice acting this time, of course - not just grunts and murmurs and hyahs. But even when retroactively adding new things, Nintendo wanted to ensure the remake's cast matched the original's pretty faithfully, so the developer held blind auditions that eventually paved the way for one actor to reprise their role during Link's adventure.

"We felt that if we were going to improve the graphics so dramatically, the cutscenes needed to be fully voiced to match," director HokWai Ng explained in the most recent Ask The Developer blog. "But at the same time, we knew we shouldn't mess with established perceptions of how certain characters sound based on the original. Navi's "Listen!" is one example. Even someone who's never played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may have heard it before. We absolutely didn't want to change anything as iconic as that."

To maintain the original's nostalgic sounds and voices, Nintendo held blind auditions with the goal of finding actors who could recreate the "feel of the original game."

Series director Eiji Aonuma recalls that the team wanted to choose actors "based solely on which voices most closely resembled those of the original." And, who woulda guessed? "As fate would have it, one of the actors we selected had actually voiced the same character in the Nintendo 64 version. None of us saw that coming."

The duo didn't outright name which character they're talking about, but fans have long been speculating that Kaori Mizuhashi might be reprising her role as Link's trusty fairy companion Navi - at least, in the Japanese language version. A leaked online video of the game's credits now also confirms that Mizuhashi is back almost three decades later. I suppose it only makes sense that the person who most closely resembles Navi is Navi.

Chris Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

title: World of Warcraft: Forever hotfix puts a stop to super speedy flag carriers that were dominating PvP battlegrounds
author: Connor Makar
content:
Cowabungle.

World of Warcraft: Forever has received its first major hotfix patch, which among other things has put an end to an especially powerful bug that made PvP battlegrounds like Warsong Gulch favoured to the Horde's advantage.

While Taurens are running, they gradually build up stacks of increased movement speed. They gain a two percent movement speed bonus per stack, and it stacks up to 30 times. That means a Tauren can gain 60 percent increased movement speed, though it's worth noting that when they stop moving, these stacks decrease. In short, cows run fast.

The Hotfix, detailed in this Blizzard blog post, stops the Tauren's plainsrunning passive from stacking during a battleground's preparation phase. What players were doing to exploit this was running back and forth in the minutes before the Warsong Gulch battleground let both teams loose. It's a capture the flag game mode, so once the gates opened, Taurens were sprinting ahead of everyone else, allowing them to quickly push towards the enemy base for a potential early flag capture.

In addition, the hotfix removes any plainsrunning stacks from Taurens once they pick up the enemy flag, and prevents them from gaining stacks while the flag is in their possession. The goal of the enemy team is to stop and kill the enemy flag carrier as soon as possible, so a Tauren moving far faster than any of your team made this pretty difficult.

Tauren's could be tanky warriors or druids too, which further added to the difficulty in killing them. With this change they're now easier to lock down, though it's worth noting a Tauren can still make use of Plainsrunning to rush into the enemy base early. They just don't have that wild speed boost from the jump.

Surely this was the only reason my Alliance Warsong Gulch games were all lost this morning, and not because my faction is for chumps. In other World of Warcraft: Forever news, the launch earlier this week was applauded as one of the smoothest in the series history, save for a few broken boats and zeppelins.

The hotfix has also decreased the respawn time of the NPC Deathstalker Erland who is needed for an escort quest. People were mulling around his spawn and wasting away while waiting for him to respawn. Also, supply vendors on the Zephras Isle have been stocked with handy tradeskill bags that you could find in other starter zones. It's the shipping I assume, it takes a while for stock to make it all the way up there.

title: Valve explains why it's running behind on Steam game approvals, asks developers to perform basic release checks to prevent re-reviews
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Approve yourself.

In the wake of witnessing an unprecedented number of game submissions to Steam over the last few months, Valve has been forced to delay approvals in order to deal with the existing backlog.

Following complaints by game developers on social media and elsewhere, Valve has now responded to explain why it's taking longer to get games approved. The short version: re-reviews are clogging up the system.

"We aim to test every game build in a timely manner, typically within three-five business days," Valve wrote in a Steam post. "However, we're running a little behind right now and taking up to 12 business days. Much of that delay is due to having to re-review games, which isn't great for you or for us."

As Valve explained in the post, games need to be re-reviewed when they're rejected for missing key quality assurance checks. In an effort to make it easier for developers to get it right the first time, Valve updated the Steam release checklist to include new, tighter requirements.

These include a requirement to run the game through Steam for at least five minutes. According to Valve, some of the games submitted have not been played through Steam.

"This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam," Valve explained.

Valve is also making it a rule to mention whether the game requires common redistributables such as DirectX, Visual C++, .NET, XNA. While Steam can automatically install many common redistributables, it needs to know which ones are needed (if any). There are also new rules about achievement readiness, cloud save detection, and some updates to Steam store page requirements.

"We now surface some of the most common issues we see missed, along with asking for some information to help our reviewers from the start," Valve added. "For example, if your game offers multiple languages and you've indicated that on your store page, we'll ask you to ensure you've included them in your build".

While Valve did not directly name gen-AI as a potential reason for this rise in the number of poor submissions, it's clear the Steam company needs to find a way to deal with the massive number of AI-assisted games.

Valve recently addressed Steam's AI game cloning problem by suggesting developers make their games less copyable. Incidentally, some of the developers whose game approvals are delayed now fear their games will be cloned by others using gen-AI and land a Steam page before the original article has made it out of submission.

title: Under pressure, Big Walk developer House House apologises for using generative AI "sparingly" while making its hit 2026 game
author: Robert Purchese
content:
"It has become a matter of public interest."

Australian developer House House has revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" to help make celebrated, indie, multiplayer puzzle game Big Walk.

In a statement sent to Aftermath - following a judging fallout related to the Independent Games Festival - House House revealed it had used large language models primarily to help debug the game's code.

"In the final stretch of Big Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," the developer said. "In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code - we'd estimate that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

House House added: "The primary use case for House House's use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code."

The studio's revelation comes after a sizeable number of IGF jurors - 19 of them - issued a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI during its development. This was done after seeing "a significant increase" in entry submissions involving generative AI use, which "set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools". And rather than not vote for these in silence, a collection of jurors decided to take a public stand.

House House hadn't disclosed Big Walk generative AI use anywhere before disclosing it for its IGF submission. "We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage," the studio explained. "We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest."

House House added: "This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable'. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to video games and our world, and apologise that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards.

"Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

It's a revelation that's likely to leave a taint of some degree on one of this year's brightest stars - a game Eurogamer awarded a full five stars to in its Big Walk review.

title: Warren Spector pops off at EA executives and their massive payouts as BioWare shuts down: "Is there any accountability left in this world?"
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
"Obviously not."

It's only been two weeks since we last heard Warren Spector sound off about EA's sudden decision to close BioWare, following the publisher's acquisition by Saudi Arabia's PIF and venture capitalist concerns. But now, the storied developer is back and - apparently - angrier than ever.

"I recently posted my thoughts about EA’s shuttering of BioWare," Spector wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "Those of you who read my post know that I was unhappy. I remain so. The tragedy of so many layoffs the last few years hasn’t been lost on me, but for some reason, BioWare hit me on an emotional level that nothing before had. I felt gut-punched."

Spector goes on to counter the idea that the studio was closed down as a "sound business decision" because the "studio’s glory days (artistic and commercial) were behind them" and that "businesses don’t succeed on history alone". These reactions, more than anything else, appear to be what's inspired Spector to take to posting again - he simply cannot agree with this assessment.

"If studio-level people leave, resulting in dilution of talent, someone is creating an environment that pushes them out. Do those culture-killers pay any price? If executives misread the market, over-hire, or make decisions that result in under-funded, over-funded, poorly-marketed games do they lose sleep let alone jobs?" he asks.

"Do those same executives suffer like developers when the needs of financial partners and private investors take precedence over the people who actually create value, let alone over the interests of players? Does anyone up there in or adjacent to the C-suite care? Is there any accountability left in this world? Obviously not."

He then goes on to list the yearly payouts that some of the highest-level executives at EA are rewarded per annum. These include:

  • Andrew Wilson (chief executive officer): $38.65 million
  • Laura Miele (president)t: $13.7 million
  • Stuart Canfield (chief financial officer): $11.3 million
  • Jake Schatz (chief legal officer): $8.4 million
  • Mala Singh (chief people officer): $8.3 million

"Tens of thousands of do-ers and makers are out of work and these people think they're worth that kind of compensation?" continues Spector. "And if you think this is a discussion about 'sound business decisions', I hope you never get anywhere near running a business. Or at least that people have the sense not to go work for you."

Back in August, we saw Warren Spector announce his intention to retire from the world of video game development. Spector's announcement comes shortly after the last game he worked on - Thick as Thieves - had its final major update only a few months after its release. Despite its charm and low price, Thick as Thieves sadly didn't sell what it needed to, resulting in layoffs at Spector's studio.

title: Eight years ago the idea of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel had me captivated, but in 2026, I find myself wondering whether Bethesda can recapture the magic
author: Chris Tapsell
content:
Eight years ago, I sat at my desk enthralled. Bethesda had just released the first trailer for The Elder Scrolls 6, a then mysteriously nameless, locationless sequel to one of the biggest games of all time, and I reckoned I'd just found the secrets to both. It was going to be set in the region of Hammerfell, I reckoned. And the city of Sentinel was a crucial factor in reasoning why.

Admittedly, I'm maybe a little more horrified at my level of Elder Scrolls obsession than I am chuffed at any apparent clairvoyance. Ultimately it was a bit of a punt, launched off the back of a day's worth of fanatical hyperfocus and exactly the right amount of the old Gamer Network office's weapons-grade filter coffee. "There's not really a lot to go on here", I wrote, sagely, "but, if we had to, we'd plant our flag in Hammerfell as the location of The Elder Scrolls 6."

Indulge me a bit and let's retread the reasoning. First, three assumptions were required in order to make any kind of guess at all: The Elder Scrolls 6 would not be set in all of Tamriel; not set outside of Tamriel; and would be set somewhere vaguely close in the timeline to the events of Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim - so as to make that bit of scrabbly rock and ruined castle, visible in that now infamous first teaser, at least somewhat traceable with contemporary descriptions in the lore.

Then came a lot of narrowing down. Not Morrowind, Cyrodiil, Skyrim or the Summerset Isles, I decided, as we'd been to all of those too recently (I'll leave it up to you whether another eight years since Morrowind lets that one still count as remotely "recent", but still). And then not Valenwood, Elsweyr, or Black Marsh, thanks to the topography of the land in the trailer and the type of environment on show. That left High Rock and Hammerfell, the former of which we ruled out because of its relative size - on the small side for a presumably beefy new TES game - and more importantly, the architecture that seemed at odds with the sandy stone just barely visible in the structures of that first teaser.

And finally: Sentinel. The city was perfectly positioned - along a coast with the sea to the right, dry mountains in the foreground, warm stone ruins to the left, no visible land beyond. Now, that setting is all but confirmed - "all but" as, technically, nothing's set in stone yet, pardon the pun. All we've since been shown is a sand dune, an Elder Scroll, the name Sentinel, and a brief quote from a Moth Priest to a Hammerfell High Queen. But we can pretty much lock it in.

To the Elder Scrolls obsessive who spent that day eight years ago scurrying down endless YouTube rabbit holes and lingering on the dustiest unofficial wiki pages, the thought of a game set there ought to be tantalising. Already, even with that paper thin new teaser, there's enough to start picking at. The new trailer's quote is dated just four years after the events of Skyrim, for instance, with both that territory and Cyrodiil located right next door, making for some lovely opportunities for crossovers and references to wider events. And the quote itself is curious. As our guides team have already speculated, the notion of "A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate" gives off the faintest whiff of a time-forking Dragon Break. That being the timeline-branching, multiple-player-choice-enabling thing that happened at the end of The Elder Scrolls 2: Daggerfall, a game which took place - aha! - in the Iliac Bay between High Rock and Hammerfell. Surely, the same bay we're looking at in that original TES 6 trailer.

It keeps going! The "victory" mentioned in that quote could refer to the victory won by the people of Hammerfell against a Thalmor invasion, in a conflict that - ooh! - took place around the same time Skyrim's main story was happening, and just a few years before that quote is dated. Could we get branching timelines? A tying together of the overarching Thalmor plotline that's been simmering away until now? A load of varying endings, as Bethesda experimented with so openly in Starfield? I'm off again. Fire up the Unofficial Elder Scrolls Pages!

There's such magic here, far beyond the apparent mastery Bethesda has over theory-baiting teasers for suckers like me. These games, for instance, also have an uncanny knack for joyful stupidity. There are Oblivion NPC barks out there that landed right as YouTube's golden era hit liftoff, and in turn defined an entire generation's sense of humour. I was once in a Slack channel here called #reeblereeblereeble, which was just myself and two other writers punting Imperial Watch taunts at each other to lighten the mood every couple of weeks, or whenever someone seemed a bit stressed. When I leave a gathering of old school friends I still catch myself bidding them "farewell!" with Wood Elf gusto, and giggling at the thought of being immediately squished into mulch.

And none of that is to mention the design itself, which has at times been more or less unparalleled. The clockwork, systemic magic of Morrowind is extraordinary, the first hour alone a lesson - at least as important as good old over-cited Mario 1:1 - in instructional design. Within a walkable radius of the musty little settlement of Seyda Neen Bethesda gave the player every tool necessary for understanding - and subsequently playing with, then outright breaking - its entire world. With Oblivion it brought the role-playing open world to the masses. With Skyrim it expanded what our very concept of the masses means.

By all accounts I should, then, be absolutely drooling at the thought of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. But for some reason the excitement is muted. It's been like this since long before this second teaser, frankly, and for much of that time I've put it down to Bethesda itself.

Bethesda Game Studios has not been on a good run. Fallout 76 might've finally recovered from its nightmarish launch, but time hasn't been hugely kind to Fallout 4, which longer-running fans have come to generally settle on as decent, but something of a slight step back from the wilder, more playful tendencies of Fallout 3 and Obsidian's New Vegas. The same could be argued of Skyrim, a wonderful game in its own right that did, nevertheless, sand down some of The Elder Scrolls' signature RPG elements into something smoother, almost closer to a frictionless modern action game (a topic on which Elder Scrolls fans have some rather strong opinions, though that's a whole other debate). And then there's Starfield, a perfectly alright game that, by virtue of that, is sort of a disaster. Its mere adequacy has only served to harden the belief, amongst long-running fans, that Bethesda has lost its magic touch.

The natural question, then, is can Bethesda recapture the magic? Again for some time I've been worried the answer might be 'no'. I worried about the BioWare-ification of the studio: the failed (albeit very well recovered) live service punt, the wonky new IP, the consolidation beneath changing owners, the shifting goalposts, the creeping corporate-ification and apparently inevitable entropy of big, creative RPG studios over a long enough period of time. The Bethesda of today is not the Bethesda of Morrowind, Oblivion or Skyrim. It's probably not even the Bethesda of Starfield. And worryingly, it's shown for some time now that it seems to care more for broad appeal - that mirage of financial success - over having caché with its long-running fans. That kind of blinkered thinking always comes back to bite.

But that's not it. I worried about that, but then I learned to stop worrying about that. The reality is Bethesda can absolutely recover the magic, just as any studio can - including BioWare for that matter, had it been given a clear, EA nonsense-free chance - for the obvious reason that no two development cycles need ever be the same. Development studios are not individuals, they're not sportspeople who go in or out of form, or see the talent fade as their legs start to give out. They're massive organisations full of all kinds of people. And so just as people leave, other people can join. There are always systemic issues at work, but you can overcome those if you can hire well, design well, plan well - if your owners are smart enough to let you, if you're given enough runway, and your leaders know what they're doing. Good game development, like just about anything done with a large team, is ultimately about making good decisions consistently over time. This is entirely possible for Bethesda to do, with the right people in charge to make them. That goes for the people above Bethesda's top brass, too.

Will Bethesda deliver? Yes, no, maybe. In a way it's besides the point. Instead, I've realised the thing that gives me pause, before burrowing giddily down into another warren of silly Tamriel backstory, is that the world this Elder Scrolls game will launch into will just be so thoroughly different to the last. Every video game from a western, triple-A publisher is life-or-death now. Every sales figure, metascore, or stray quote is another algorithmically driven hate-narrative, a collective Emperor's thumbs down. And every ultimate owner of these games now seems to be properly set on being really impossible not to loathe.

Bethesda can't make games that are just alright, because today alright means doom. It takes too long, for one - we're already well into GTA 6 territory here, 15 years on from Skyrim and counting, with master of whispers Jason Schreier suggesting at least another two to go. And by virtue of that, its games must surely cost too much. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel will sell gangbusters, which will mitigate that. But at this level of spending, the level of the stratosphere, a sales hit alone arguably isn't enough. The world demands something more.

You take that long and cost that much and your game has to shake the mountains and rumble the earth. Move the industry or revive it. Sell physical consoles that are likely to cost into the low thousands. Rewrite a narrative of failure, incompetence, arrogance, waste, and decline. This is not me declaring those things necessary; it's the way of the industry now. The sands have shifted. A game like The Elder Scrolls 6 is now a symbol. In this case one of its owner, Xbox.

That company has no other cards to play but this one, as evidenced by CEO Asha Sharma jangling her Todd Howard-shaped keys every time the heat from all that delicious bloodletting gets a little much. Sentinel has to not only be successful, then, but widely adored. Anything else, after hundreds of millions on its development, billions on wider acquisitions, thousands upon thousands of layoffs (and, let's not forget, a boycott derived from still blood-splattered links to what a UN commission calls a genocide), will be a failure. Not a failure for Bethesda's developers, by any stretch, but for the company at large after the weight of context Xbox has dropped on top of them. A failure to flip over the table at the dying moment of a losing game. A failure for those who are all too desperate to change the story.

All this - all the perpetual, seemingly endless turmoil of making video games, the cynicism in the air of so many gaming spaces, the terminally compromised corporate ownership of the games themselves - is what makes excitement so hard to muster. I look at The Elder Scrolls now and can't help but feel a little tinge of anger or sadness. Anger that yet another route to open joy - and to unserious teen memories and, frankly, a tiny little part of a personal identity, no matter how hard I try to resist that - has become wound up with such unsavoury ownership. All this, reduced to yet another PR tool and distraction technique to shift eyes and words away from bleak and pointless cruelty. And then sadness, at the idea I might escape into it, whenever it finally arrives, only to find myself in exactly the world I wish I could just briefly leave behind. Bethesda's developers can recapture the magic. But can the world of video games let them?

title: Square Enix accidentally botches a Nier: Automata update, balloons required file size from 50GB to 366GB on PC, but don't worry, there's a fix
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
"Do you think games are silly little things?"

Yesterday, Nier: Automata received a new patch on Steam, adding more language support to the title - it can now be played with Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese options - but this new update also, somehow, inflated the file size of the game on PC from about 50GB to 366GB. D'oh! What's worse is, the update is not optional.

The cause of this, reportedly, is a bug that caused all the DLC in the YoRHa Edition of the game to become the same size as the base game - and the new download stacks them all concurrently. "Only SquareEnix can turn 40GB into 366GB with 8GB patch," says one dissatisfied Steam reviewer.

If you don't have space for this massive new file on your PC (and I can't say I blame you, it's ridiculous), there is a workaround, as confirmed by Square Enix in a tweet via its Japanese Twitter account.

"We have confirmed an issue where, following the latest update to the Steam version of Nier: Automata, the installation process indicates that more storage space is required than expected," noted the publisher. "We are currently investigating the cause and working on a solution. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. As a temporary workaround, you can download the base game by unchecking the DLC under Steam → Properties → DLC."

It's quite ironic, really, that so many Steam reviewers are complaining about things like "I just need to delete 90% of my computer to install this" when a large part of the game is managing the software/programmes installed on your android protagonists in order to upgrade your abilities and stats. There's even an ending for uninstalling your OS on your mechanical main characters. I'd be inclined to suggest this is some sort of meta psy-op from creator Yoko Taro, but… nah, that's just fantasy, isn't it? Isn't it?

Speaking of Taro, earlier this year we learned that "Nier Automata will continue", though we only heard back in 2025 that most of the projects the developer was working on were cancelled. One of these may have been the Tencent-backed Nier mobile game in 2024, which reportedly "struggled to find a monetisation to offset its high costs."

title: Humble Bundle redesign removes two-factor verification from settings
author: Jay Peters
content:
Jay Peters

is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The Humble Bundle storefront for buying games and other software recently got a new look, but on the settings page, it no longer offers a way to add or update two-factor verification methods, as reported by Kotaku. PC Gamer also points out that there are Humble Bundle support pages discussing two-factor verification, and the writer for the publication said that they had set up two-factor verification on the old version of the site.

However, it does appear that, at least as of now, there is some form of two-factor verification. When I tried logging into my Humble Bundle account while writing this article, I was prompted to check my email for an access code before I could access my account. While logged in, I was able to update my password, but I didn’t have to enter my old password to be able to do so.

For what it’s worth, my passwords app also shows that I set up a rotating two-factor code for Humble Bundle at some point. I was not asked to input that at any part of my login process today.

Humble Bundle owner IGN Entertainment and IGN parent company Ziff Davis didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
